title: Standard-Borel Real Codings and Determining Classes

items.title: Hilbert cube has a bimeasurable real coding
items.statement: There is an explicit measurable bijection c from [0,1]^N onto a Borel subset C of [0,1], with measurable inverse. Both domains have their Borel sigma-algebras.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: For x in [0,1], encode t=x/2 in [0,1/2] by b_k(t)=floor(2^k t)-2 floor(2^(k-1)t), k>=1. Each digit is Borel, the expansion has infinitely many zeros, and t=sum b_k 2^-k; the latter follows from 0<=t-2^-k floor(2^k t)<2^-k. Conversely any binary row with infinitely many zeros and sum <=1/2 is this canonical expansion of a unique t. This row condition is Borel: intersect over N the union over k>=N of {b_k=0}, and intersect with the closed sum constraint. Index cube coordinates by i>=0 and row digits by k>=1. Put j=2^i(2(k-1)+1), the explicit bijection J(i,k-1) from thm-n-cross-n-countable onto the positive integers. Interleave by a_j=b_k(x_i/2), then send a to sum_{j>=1} 2a_j 3^-j. This last map is a homeomorphism from binary sequence space onto the closed ternary Cantor set: first differing digit dominates the tail, and agreeing on the first n digits gives distance <=3^-n; recover digits by the separated closed ternary cylinders. Its image C consists exactly of codes whose every deinterleaved row satisfies the preceding Borel condition, hence is Borel. The inverse has coordinates twice the convergent binary sums, each Borel by lim; the countable rational-box basis of the cube shows coordinate measurability suffices. The cube Borel sigma-algebra equals its product sigma-algebra by this countable basis. No arbitrary binary expansion or omitted image-measurability claim is allowed.

items.title: Standard borel spaces admit bimeasurable real codings
items.statement: Assume AC. Every standard-Borel space (E,S) is measurably isomorphic to a Borel subset of [0,1]. The empty space is included.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: Choose the one Polish presentation supplied by the definition. Apply Hilbert-cube universality to P, and the forward Alexandrov theorem to its completely metrizable image in the cube; the image is G_delta and hence Borel. Compose with c. Since c inverse is measurable, c[B]=(c inverse)^-1[B] is Borel in C for every Borel B in the cube; C itself is Borel in R. Both restrictions are measurable. This uses only the forward embedding/G_delta interfaces, not arbitrary product probability, inner regularity, or the defective converse of any recorded catalogue statement. AC covers inherited metric/countability choices. Supply the cube metric explicitly by the weighted-product lemma. In the Alexandrov proof, each point in every G_n lies within 1/n of a point of Y because the n-small neighbourhood meets Y and has ambient diameter <1/n; hence intersection G_n already lies in closure Y and equals Y. The current published proof now explicitly includes this ambient-closure argument; the authored proof checks that repaired interface. AC gives the DC selection there by choosing a successor for each admissible finite partial construction and iterating it on N.

items.title: Standard borel spaces have countable generating and measure determining algebras
items.statement: Under AC a standard-Borel space has a countable algebra that generates its sigma-algebra, separates points, and determines every finite measure: agreement of two finite measures on this algebra implies equality. In particular it determines probability measures.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: Pull back rational closed rays intersected with the code image; include E. By thm-rationals-countable, enumerate this countable family as (H_n). Let A_n be the Boolean algebra generated by H_0,...,H_(n-1). Its atoms are the at most 2^n intersections of the n choices H_i or H_i^c, and each member of A_n is a union of those atoms, so A_n is finite. The Boolean algebra A generated by all rational cuts is union_n A_n; thm-countable-union-of-countable makes it countable. Rational cuts separate codes, and the real Borel generator theorem gives generation. The equality class of two finite measures of the same total mass is a lambda-system containing A. Apply pi-lambda. Finiteness is essential; do not assert determination for arbitrary infinite measures. Closed left rays are complements of the rational right rays in the published generator theorem.
items.axiom_use: AC supplies the countable-choice instance of def-countable-choice used by thm-countable-union-of-countable to pass from the finite algebras A_n to their countable union. No choice is used in the rational-cut separation or pi-lambda argument.

items.title: Borel subspaces admit polish presentations
items.statement: Under AC, each Borel subset B of a Polish space P admits a finer Polish topology with precisely its trace Borel sigma-algebra. Consequently it is standard Borel under the published Polish-presentation definition.

references.title: Rao and Srivastava, An Elementary Proof of the Borel Isomorphism Theorem
Marker, Descriptive Set Theory, Lemmas 2.22-2.23 and Theorem 2.24

items.strategy: Prove the stronger refinement assertion: every Borel B in P is clopen for a finer Polish topology on P with the same Borel sets. Open B works by the topological sum of B and its closed complement: open subsets are G_delta, so have complete compatible metrics; bound these by 1 and put distance 2 between components. For countably many such refinements tau_n, include the original topology tau_0 and identify their common refinement with the diagonal in the product of (P,tau_n). Equality of coordinates is closed because every map to the original Hausdorff P is continuous. The complete product metric restricts to a complete metric, and countable bases imply separability under AC. Every basic open set is old Borel and the basis is countable, so the refinement has exactly the old Borel sets. The union of the B_n is open in this common refinement; split it from its closed complement as before to make it clopen. Complements require no further change. Thus refinable sets form a sigma-algebra containing the open sets. Restrict the resulting complete metric to the clopen B. AC is used for countably many witnesses/metrics/bases. This fills the definition seam without Lusin-Souslin or a perfect-set theorem.

title: Standard-Borel Real Codings and Determining Classes: Examples

items.title: Countable discrete spaces are standard borel
items.statement: Every at most countable discrete measurable space, with its full power set, is standard Borel, including the empty space.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: The discrete 0/1 metric is complete because a Cauchy sequence is eventually constant. The whole countable set is dense, and all subsets are open.

items.title: Euclidean borel spaces are standard borel
items.statement: For each finite n, (R^n,B(R^n)) is standard Borel.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: Use the maximum coordinate metric. Completeness is coordinatewise real completeness, and Q^n is countable dense. Include n=0 as a singleton.

items.title: Borel subspaces of polish spaces are standard borel
items.statement: Under AC, each Borel subset of a Polish space is standard Borel, even if its inherited topology is not Polish.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: Apply the refinement lemma. The rationals inside R are a concrete example: the countable discrete topology provides a Polish presentation of the same full power-set measurable structure. No claim that the inherited rational topology is complete is used.

items.title: Conditional expectation given a sigma algebra
items.statement: On a probability space (Omega,F,P), for a real X in L1(P) and sub-sigma-algebra G, a conditional-expectation version is a G-measurable real integrable Y with integral_A Y = integral_A X for every A in G. No completeness of G is assumed.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.title: Conditional expectation exists by radon nikodym
items.statement: Assume AC (used in the supplied RN construction). For every X and G as in the definition, a conditional-expectation version exists.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: On (Omega,G), set nu_plus(A)=integral_A X+ and nu_minus(A)=integral_A X-. Both are finite positive measures absolutely continuous relative to the probability P restricted to G; the common finite exhaustion is Omega. Apply RN separately, test negative-level sets to make densities nonnegative a.e., replace their exceptional G-null sets by zero, and use total masses to show both densities integrable. Their difference is the required real integrable version. No infinity minus infinity occurs. The published RN proof passes through the finite-positive part of the Lebesgue decomposition theorem, where a sequence approaching a supremum and countably many Hahn decompositions are selected; AC is explicitly assumed here to cover those choices. Finite integral implies finite density a.e.; replace each G-measurable infinite-value null set by zero before subtracting.
items.axiom_use: AC inherited through RN existence: choose a maximizing sequence and countably many Hahn decompositions in its finite-measure proof. No claim of optimal choice strength; algebraic properties of already supplied versions require no additional choice.

items.title: Conditional expectation is unique almost surely
items.statement: Two conditional-expectation versions of the same integrable X given G agree P-a.s.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: Their difference is G-measurable and integrable. Its integral over each G-event vanishes. Test the positive and negative sets, using the nonnegative-zero-integral criterion.

items.title: Conditional expectation as an ae class
items.statement: Under AC, with existence supplied by the chosen Radon-Nikodym proof: E[X|G] denotes the unique L1(Omega,G,P restricted to G) class of versions. Equality and inequalities between conditional expectations are a.s. assertions. The input can equally be an ambient L1 class, since a.e.-equal inputs have identical event integrals.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.axiom_use: AC inherited through RN existence: choose a maximizing sequence and countably many Hahn decompositions in its finite-measure proof. No claim of optimal choice strength; algebraic properties of already supplied versions require no additional choice.

items.title: Basic algebra and order properties of conditional expectation
items.statement: Under AC, with existence supplied by the chosen Radon-Nikodym proof: For real integrable X,Y and scalars a,b, conditional expectation is linear, positive and order preserving, fixes constants, preserves expectation, and |E[X|G]|<=E[|X||G] a.s. Moreover X<Y a.s. implies E[X|G]<E[Y|G] a.s.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: Test the proposed linear combination and constants in the defining event integrals and invoke uniqueness. Negative discrepancy sets prove positivity and order; apply order to -|X|<=X<=|X|. Take A=Omega for expectation preservation. For strict order set W=Y-X>0 a.s., V=E[W|G]>=0. On A={V=0}, integral_A W=0 forces P(A)=0. This corrects the impossible a.s. reading of the requested strict-inequality counterexample.
items.axiom_use: AC inherited through RN existence: choose a maximizing sequence and countably many Hahn decompositions in its finite-measure proof. No claim of optimal choice strength; algebraic properties of already supplied versions require no additional choice.

items.title: Taking out what is known
items.statement: Under AC, with existence supplied by the chosen Radon-Nikodym proof: For bounded real G-measurable Z and X in L1, E[ZX|G]=Z E[X|G] a.s. The identity extends to finite real G-measurable Z whenever ZX and Z E[X|G] are integrable; in fact X,ZX in L1 already imply the latter integrability.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: First indicators by intersecting test events, then bounded simple functions by linearity, then bounded measurable factors by simple approximation and DCT. For the stronger integrability observation put U=E[|X||G] and Z_n=min(|Z|,n). The bounded identity and expectation preservation give E[Z_n U]=E[Z_n |X|]. MCT gives E[|Z|U]=E|ZX|<infinity. Since |E[X|G]|<=U, the needed product is integrable. Finally truncate signed Z and apply ordinary DCT to both event integrals. This route avoids a forward appeal to conditional MCT.
items.axiom_use: AC inherited through RN existence: choose a maximizing sequence and countably many Hahn decompositions in its finite-measure proof. No claim of optimal choice strength; algebraic properties of already supplied versions require no additional choice.

items.title: Tower property of conditional expectation
items.statement: Under AC, with existence supplied by the chosen Radon-Nikodym proof: If H subset G subset F, then E[E[X|G]|H]=E[X|H] and E[E[X|H]|G]=E[X|H] a.s.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: For the first identity test each H-event twice. For the second the H-measurable representative is already G-measurable and satisfies its own defining identity.
items.axiom_use: AC inherited through RN existence: choose a maximizing sequence and countably many Hahn decompositions in its finite-measure proof. No claim of optimal choice strength; algebraic properties of already supplied versions require no additional choice.

items.title: Conditioning a known variable and an independent variable
items.statement: Under AC, with existence supplied by the chosen Radon-Nikodym proof: A G-measurable integrable X satisfies E[X|G]=X. If P({X in B} intersect A)=P(X in B)P(A) for every Borel B and A in G, then E[X|G]=EX.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: The known case is immediate from event integrals. For the independent case prove E[X 1_A]=EX P(A) first for indicators of Borel sets of X, then simple functions of X, then positive and negative parts by simple approximation and MCT. This states and uses independence directly; no unnecessary factorization theorem or product-measure edge is imported.
items.axiom_use: AC inherited through RN existence: choose a maximizing sequence and countably many Hahn decompositions in its finite-measure proof. No claim of optimal choice strength; algebraic properties of already supplied versions require no additional choice.

items.title: Conditional expectation for nonnegative variables
items.statement: Assume AC for selecting countably many versions. For measurable X:Omega->[0,infinity], define E[X|G] as the a.s. class of the increasing limit of versions of E[min(X,n)|G], after making them nonnegative and increasing off one G-null set. Values infinity are allowed. Well-definedness and arbitrary increasing truncations are justified next.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.axiom_use: AC covers inherited RN existence and the countable selection of conditional versions; the proof removes one measurable countable union of order-exception sets.

items.title: Conditional monotone convergence
items.statement: Under AC, the extended conditional expectation is the unique a.s. class of nonnegative G-measurable Y with integral_A Y=integral_A X for every A in G. If 0<=X_n increases to X a.s., E[X_n|G] increases to E[X|G] a.s.; bounded integrable truncating approximations give the same class.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: MCT on both sides of the defining identity proves that the truncation limit represents X. Extended uniqueness must not subtract infinite integrals: on A={Y>=Z+1/k, Z<=m}, integration of Z is bounded by m and equality of event integrals forces Y integrable there, so the difference test gives P(A)=0. Union over positive k,m covers {Y>Z}; interchange Y,Z. Order follows by the same finite-localization test applied to two represented nonnegative measures. Select countably many versions using AC, delete their G-null exceptional order sets, pass to the increasing limit by MCT and apply extended uniqueness. For a.s. rather than pointwise input monotonicity use the invariance of nonnegative integrals under a.e. equality, proved by null-set integrals.
items.axiom_use: AC covers inherited RN existence and the countable selection of conditional versions; the proof removes one measurable countable union of order-exception sets.

items.title: Conditional fatou and dominated convergence
items.statement: Under AC, for nonnegative X_n, E[liminf X_n|G]<=liminf E[X_n|G] a.s. For real X_n converging a.s. to X with |X_n|<=W in L1, E[X_n|G] converges to E[X|G] a.s. and in L1.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: Apply conditional MCT to inf_{k>=n} X_k and use conditional order. Apply Fatou to W+X_n and W-X_n to trap liminf and limsup. Ordinary DCT applies to the conditional versions dominated by E[W|G] after one common null set, and supplies L1 convergence. No kernel theorem is used.
items.axiom_use: AC inherited through RN existence: choose a maximizing sequence and countably many Hahn decompositions in its finite-measure proof. No claim of optimal choice strength; algebraic properties of already supplied versions require no additional choice.

items.title: Convex functions have countable supporting line representations
items.statement: A finite convex function phi on R is the supremum of its supporting lines at rational points, using the left derivative as the deterministic slope. The coefficients need not be rational.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: For rational q set ell_q(t)=phi(q)+phi_left_derivative(q)(t-q). Supporting lines lie below phi. Secant inequalities bound all slopes on each compact interval contained in a larger interval and imply local Lipschitz continuity. For q tending to x, bounded slopes and continuity imply ell_q(x) tends to phi(x). This also covers irrational-slope affine functions, for which restricting both coefficients to rationals would fail.

items.title: Conditional jensen inequality
items.statement: Under AC, with existence supplied by the chosen Radon-Nikodym proof: If X and phi(X) are integrable and phi:R->R is finite convex, then phi(E[X|G])<=E[phi(X)|G] a.s.; the left side is integrable.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: Use each countably indexed supporting affine line, linearity and order. Discard the countable union of exceptional sets, then take the supremum. A fixed supporting line bounds the negative part of phi(E[X|G]) by an integrable affine expression, and the conditional upper bound controls its positive part. No uncountable null-set union or regular conditional distribution is permitted.
items.axiom_use: AC inherited through RN existence: choose a maximizing sequence and countably many Hahn decompositions in its finite-measure proof. No claim of optimal choice strength; algebraic properties of already supplied versions require no additional choice.

items.title: Absolute real powers are Borel measurable and convex
items.statement: For every real p>=1, the function phi_p:R->R, phi_p(t)=|t|^p, is finite, Borel measurable, and convex.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.
van der Vaart, Martingales, Diffusions and Financial Mathematics

items.strategy: For p>=1, thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives and thm-algebra-of-derivatives give (u^p)'=p u^(p-1) and (u^p)''=p(p-1)u^(p-2)>=0 on (0,infinity); cor-second-derivative-characterises-convexity gives convexity there, and thm-monotonicity-from-the-derivative gives monotonicity. For 0<u<=1, log u<=0 and p log u<=log u by thm-natural-logarithm-laws; strict increase and positivity of exp give 0<=u^p<=u. The squeeze theorem therefore extends continuity to 0, and the endpoint limit extends the half-line convex inequality to [0,infinity). The triangle inequality gives |lambda x+(1-lambda)y|<=lambda|x|+(1-lambda)|y|; monotonicity followed by half-line convexity proves the defining convexity inequality for phi_p on R. The continuous absolute-value and power pieces make phi_p continuous, so thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel and def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces give Borel measurability.

items.title: Conditional lp contraction
items.statement: Under AC, with existence supplied by the chosen Radon-Nikodym proof: For 1<=p<=infinity, conditional expectation maps real Lp(P) into Lp(P restricted to G) with norm at most one.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: For finite p, lem-absolute-real-powers-are-convex supplies the finite Borel-measurable convex function phi(t)=|t|^p required by conditional Jensen; then preserve expectation. For infinity apply conditional order to the essential bound. Finite-measure inclusion ensures X is in L1; at p=1 use the modulus bound.
items.axiom_use: AC inherited through RN existence: choose a maximizing sequence and countably many Hahn decompositions in its finite-measure proof. No claim of optimal choice strength; algebraic properties of already supplied versions require no additional choice.

items.title: Conditional expectation is the l2 orthogonal projection
items.statement: Under AC, L2(G) embeds isometrically as a closed subspace of real L2(F); E[X|G] is the orthogonal projection of X onto it. The minimizing prediction is unique as an a.s. class.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: The inclusion is an isometry and is well-defined on quotient classes. Completeness on the restricted measure space implies its image is closed; AC is inherited from selecting representatives in Riesz-Fischer. The defining identity gives zero pairing of X-E[X|G] with bounded G-simple functions. Bounded truncations approximate every G-measurable L2 variable in L2 by DCT; Cauchy-Schwarz passes pairing to the limit. Alternatively taking-out plus expectation preservation yields the same orthogonality. Expand squared norms to get the Pythagorean identity and uniqueness. No Hilbert-space projection existence theorem is needed.
items.axiom_use: AC covers inherited RN existence and the countable-choice hypothesis of restricted L2 completeness, including representative selection in Riesz-Fischer. Orthogonality uses taking-out for integrable L2 products directly.

items.title: Conditional variance
items.statement: Under AC, with existence supplied by the chosen Radon-Nikodym proof: For real X in L2, define Var(X|G)=E[(X-E[X|G])^2|G], as an a.s. class. Its integrability, nonnegativity, representative independence and second-moment formula are justified by the following lemma.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.axiom_use: AC inherited through RN existence: choose a maximizing sequence and countably many Hahn decompositions in its finite-measure proof. No claim of optimal choice strength; algebraic properties of already supplied versions require no additional choice.

items.title: Conditional variance is well-defined and has the second-moment formula
items.statement: Under AC, with existence supplied by the chosen Radon-Nikodym proof: For real X in L2, conditional variance is an integrable nonnegative class independent of the representatives, and equals E[X^2|G]-(E[X|G])^2 a.s.
items.strategy: L2 contraction makes U=E[X|G] square integrable. The inequality (X-U)^2<=2X^2+2U^2 proves integrability; Cauchy-Schwarz makes XU integrable. Changing representatives changes the square only on a measurable null set, hence does not change its conditional class. Expand the square, apply taking-out with factor U to X and known-variable conditioning to U^2; positivity gives nonnegativity.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.axiom_use: AC inherited through RN existence: choose a maximizing sequence and countably many Hahn decompositions in its finite-measure proof. No claim of optimal choice strength; algebraic properties of already supplied versions require no additional choice.

items.title: Conditional variance decomposition
items.statement: Under AC, with existence supplied by the chosen Radon-Nikodym proof: For real X in L2, Var(X)=E[Var(X|G)]+Var(E[X|G]).

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: Take expectations in the conditional second-moment identity and subtract (EX)^2. Expectation preservation identifies the mean of the conditional mean.
items.axiom_use: AC inherited through RN existence: choose a maximizing sequence and countably many Hahn decompositions in its finite-measure proof. No claim of optimal choice strength; algebraic properties of already supplied versions require no additional choice.

items.title: Uniform integrability of conditional expectations of one variable
items.statement: Under AC, with existence supplied by the chosen Radon-Nikodym proof: For fixed real X in L1, all the classes E[X|G], with G ranging over sub-sigma-algebras of F, form a uniformly integrable family.

references.title: van der Vaart, Martingales, Diffusions and Financial Mathematics

items.strategy: Put U_G=E[|X||G] and A_G={|E[X|G]|>K}. Markov from integrating K 1_A<=|E[X|G]| gives P(A_G)<=E|X|/K. The modulus bound and the defining event identity give integral_A |E[X|G]|<=integral_A |X|. Absolute continuity of the integral makes this uniformly small. The proof takes no simultaneous uncountable choice of versions.
items.axiom_use: AC inherited through RN existence: choose a maximizing sequence and countably many Hahn decompositions in its finite-measure proof. No claim of optimal choice strength; algebraic properties of already supplied versions require no additional choice.

items.title: Conditional expectation is a class not a canonical pointwise function
items.statement: Under AC, with existence supplied by the chosen Radon-Nikodym proof: Identities on this page concern a.s. classes. A finite or countable collection of identities can be enforced off one measurable null set; this statement gives no simultaneous pointwise representative for an uncountable collection. Later kernel results impose their own hypotheses.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.axiom_use: AC inherited through RN existence: choose a maximizing sequence and countably many Hahn decompositions in its finite-measure proof. No claim of optimal choice strength; algebraic properties of already supplied versions require no additional choice.

items.title: Conditional cauchy schwarz inequality
items.statement: Under AC, with existence supplied by the chosen Radon-Nikodym proof: For real X,Y in L2, |E[XY|G]|^2<=E[X^2|G]E[Y^2|G] a.s.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: Ordinary Cauchy-Schwarz makes XY integrable. Apply conditional positivity to (X+tY)^2 for rational t; outside one countable union of null sets the quadratic is nonnegative for all rational t, hence all real t by continuity. If the quadratic coefficient vanishes its linear coefficient must vanish; otherwise its discriminant is nonpositive.
items.axiom_use: AC inherited through RN existence: choose a maximizing sequence and countably many Hahn decompositions in its finite-measure proof. No claim of optimal choice strength; algebraic properties of already supplied versions require no additional choice.

items.title: Conditioning on a finite partition
items.statement: Under AC, with existence supplied by the chosen Radon-Nikodym proof: For a finite G-generating measurable partition (A_i), a version is sum_i 1_Ai integral_Ai X / P(A_i), with value zero on zero-mass cells.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: Bound its absolute integral by sum_i integral_Ai |X|. Every G-event is a union of cells, so verify each cell and add. For X=1_B the positive-cell formula is P(B intersect A_i)/P(A_i).
items.axiom_use: AC inherited through RN existence: choose a maximizing sequence and countably many Hahn decompositions in its finite-measure proof. No claim of optimal choice strength; algebraic properties of already supplied versions require no additional choice.

items.title: Conditioning on trivial and full sigma algebras
items.statement: Under AC, with existence supplied by the chosen Radon-Nikodym proof: For integrable X, E[X|{empty,Omega}]=EX and E[X|F]=X as classes.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: Check a constant in the trivial-sigma identity; the full-sigma case is the known-variable rule.
items.axiom_use: AC inherited through RN existence: choose a maximizing sequence and countably many Hahn decompositions in its finite-measure proof. No claim of optimal choice strength; algebraic properties of already supplied versions require no additional choice.

items.title: Conditioning an independent sum on one summand
items.statement: Under AC, with existence supplied by the chosen Radon-Nikodym proof: If real integrable X,Y are independent, E[X+Y|sigma(X)]=X+EY a.s.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: State independence as the Borel rectangle identity; the preimages of Borel sets under X are exactly sigma(X). Apply the independent-variable and known-variable clauses, then linearity.
items.axiom_use: AC inherited through RN existence: choose a maximizing sequence and countably many Hahn decompositions in its finite-measure proof. No claim of optimal choice strength; algebraic properties of already supplied versions require no additional choice.

items.title: Conditional expectation given a discrete random variable
items.statement: Under AC, with existence supplied by the chosen Radon-Nikodym proof: For countably valued Y and integrable X, E[X|sigma(Y)] has value integral_{Y=y} X/P(Y=y) on every positive-mass fibre, and zero on the remaining fibres.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: The countable union of null fibres is null; the piecewise function is measurable. Its L1 norm is bounded by E|X| by summing over fibres. Countable additivity of the integral proves the identity on every union of fibres.
items.axiom_use: AC inherited through RN existence: choose a maximizing sequence and countably many Hahn decompositions in its finite-measure proof. No claim of optimal choice strength; algebraic properties of already supplied versions require no additional choice.

items.title: L2 best prediction by conditional expectation
items.statement: Under AC, for X in real L2 and any Z in L2(G), E[(X-Z)^2]=E[(X-E[X|G])^2]+E[(E[X|G]-Z)^2].

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: Apply orthogonality and expand the square. Equality of errors holds precisely when Z=E[X|G] a.s.
items.axiom_use: AC inherited through RN existence: choose a maximizing sequence and countably many Hahn decompositions in its finite-measure proof. No claim of optimal choice strength; algebraic properties of already supplied versions require no additional choice.

items.title: Law of total variance
items.statement: Under AC, with existence supplied by the chosen Radon-Nikodym proof: Let Omega={0,1}^2 have its full sigma-algebra and P({(u,v)})=1/4. Set U(u,v)=u, V(u,v)=v, X=U+V and G=sigma(U). Then Var(X)=1/2, E[Var(X|G)]=1/4, Var(E[X|G])=1/4.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: The four displayed masses sum to one, so the finite-space probability theorem supplies the probability space. The rectangle calculation P(U=u,V=v)=1/4=P(U=u)P(V=v) proves the exact independence hypothesis. Hence the known-and-independent-variable lemma gives E[X|G]=U+1/2 and Var(X|G)=E[(V-1/2)^2|G]=1/4. Direct finite sums on the four atoms give Var(X)=1/2 and Var(U+1/2)=1/4.

items.title: A version can fail a pointwise identity on a null set
items.statement: Under AC, with existence supplied by the chosen Radon-Nikodym proof: The statement that every version of E[0|F] is identically zero at every sample point is false.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: Use Omega={a,b}, F its power set, P({a})=0 and P({b})=1. The indicator of {a} is F-measurable, integrable, and has zero integral on every event, yet equals one at a.

items.title: Conditioning does not preserve strict inequalities
items.statement: Under AC, with existence supplied by the chosen Radon-Nikodym proof: Pointwise strict inequalities need not hold at every point for arbitrary conditional-expectation versions. This does NOT refute preservation of strict a.s. inequalities, which is proved on the A page.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: On Omega={a,b} with masses 0,1 and G=F, take X=0, Y=1 everywhere. Choose E[X|F]=2 on a and 0 on b, and E[Y|F]=1 everywhere. The defining integrals hold, but the strict comparison fails at a. The stable requested ID is retained with an explicit pointwise scope; the impossible a.s. interpretation is rejected.

items.title: Taking out an unbounded factor needs integrability
items.statement: Under AC, with existence supplied by the chosen Radon-Nikodym proof: Dropping product integrability from the signed L1 taking-out rule can make its left side undefined, even when both factors individually are integrable.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.

items.strategy: On Omega=N_{>=1} times {-1,1} with its full sigma-algebra, put w_n=2^(-3n-1)/S, where def-integer-power and thm-geometric-series give S=sum_{n>=1}2^(-3n)=1/7. Define P as the sum over n of w_n delta_(n,-1) plus the sum over n of w_n delta_(n,1). The Dirac probability proposition and thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures make these positive weighted sums measures; their finite sum is a measure. The geometric calculation gives P(Omega)=1, hence def-probability-measure applies and P({(n,s)})=w_n. Let G=sigma(n), X(n,s)=s 2^n and Z(n,s)=2^(2n). Both E|X| and E|Z| are finite geometric series, and E[X|G]=0 by cancellation on each fibre. But ZX=s 2^(3n) has both positive and negative integrals infinite, so E[ZX|G] in the signed L1 sense is undefined although Z E[X|G]=0.
